teaser: A whole cell, a tiny package, and the kindness of soap.
title: Tiny Guests
question: How are bacteria and viruses different?
idea: Bacteria are whole living cells. Viruses carry instructions and need a living cell to make copies. Soap, scrubbing, and rinsing help lift germs away.

curiosity.intro: Two tiny guests. One big question. What makes them different?
curiosity.carryForward: Meet a cell and a package of instructions. Follow the soap, then keep a kind habit.

questions.question: Could a tiny guest be a helper?
questions.notice: A yogurt cup sits beside the oval guest in the book.
questions.say: Bacteria are whole living cells. Many help us: some live in our gut and help with food, and others help make yogurt. Some can make people unwell. We can welcome the helpers and keep our hands clean.
questions.try: Say one place where helpful bacteria can live.

questions.question: What does a virus need to make copies?
questions.notice: Compare the oval cell with the smaller round package and its coiled thread.
questions.say: A virus is not a cell. It is a tiny package of instructions in a coat. It must borrow a living cell’s machinery to make copies. Bacteria are much bigger than viruses, but both are too small to see with just your eyes.
questions.try: Finish this thought: Instructions need something to carry them out, just as a virus needs…

questions.question: How does soap help the water?
questions.notice: Little rubs the lather over both mitten hands. The towel waits beside the sink.
questions.say: Soap can pull apart the oily outer layers of many germs. Soap and scrubbing also lift germs off skin so running water can rinse them away. Plain water rinses off some, but soap helps remove more. Scrub for about 20 seconds, then rinse and dry.
questions.try: Say the commands in order: Wet. Add soap. Scrub. Rinse. Dry.

questions.question: What can your body remember?
questions.notice: Little keeps a guest’s shape in the notebook.
questions.say: Your immune system is your body’s team of defenders. Some learn to recognize germs and remember their features next time. Antibiotics are different: these medicines work on bacteria but not viruses. Each kind of help has its own job.
questions.try: Tell how learning a shape could help you recognize it again.

reading.foldableTitle: A little book of tiny guests
reading.parentNote: Age 8 / Grade 3 reading. Welcome shared reading, spoken answers, and dictation. Pause at cell, bacteria, virus, antibiotic, and immune system.

outline.arc: Little wonders about unseen guests, discovers a helpful whole cell and a smaller package of instructions, follows soap-and-rinse commands, compares antibiotics, and keeps a clue about defenders remembering.

beatIntents.intent: Establish the cozy sink, amber soap, linen towel, magnifier, book and question; the ordinary magnifier does not reveal actual germs.
Discover helpful bacteria through a yogurt cup and a large soft oval cell on a book page; keep the whole-cell idea clear.
Compare a much smaller round virus with the bacterium, and reveal its coiled instructions; a cell supplies the machinery.
Return to the sink for soap, a gentle scrub, rinse and dry; Little follows command sentences.
Revisit the paired book sketches to ask why antibiotics work on bacteria but not viruses; show no medicine or treatment action.
End with Little saving a guest shape in a notebook, echoing defenders learning and remembering, with a kind habit to keep.

beats.title: Guests beyond our eyes
beats.passage: Little Wonderer held a magnifier beside the sink. “Can I see the tiny guests on my hands?” “Germs are far too small for just our eyes,” said Big. “Even that magnifier cannot show them.” They opened a book. Bacteria and viruses waited on its pages. Were these tiny guests alike?
beats.prompt: Why did Little need the book as well as the magnifier?

beats.title: A whole little cell
beats.passage: Little paused at a yogurt cup. “Are all bacteria a problem?” “Many are helpers,” said Big. “Some live happily in your gut and help with food. Others help make yogurt. Some can make people unwell.” A bacterium is one whole living cell: a tiny unit with the parts it needs to live.
beats.prompt: What makes a bacterium a whole living cell?

beats.title: Instructions in a coat
beats.passage: The next guest was much smaller. A virus is a tiny package of instructions in a coat, not a cell. It cannot make copies alone. It must borrow a living cell’s machinery: the parts that do the work. “Like a program saying ‘copy me’?” asked Little. “Instructions that need a cell,” said Big.
beats.prompt: Why can’t a virus follow its instructions alone?

beats.title: A kind habit
beats.passage: Back at the sink, Little made a soft lather. Soap can pull apart the oily outer layers of many germs. It also loosens germs from skin. “Wet. Add soap. Scrub for 20 seconds. Rinse. Dry,” Little said. Water carried the loosened guests away. A small habit could do a lot.
beats.prompt: What do soap, scrubbing, and rinsing do?

beats.title: Different tiny guests
beats.passage: “Does one medicine work on both guests?” Little asked. Big shook their head. “An antibiotic is a medicine that works on bacteria. It does not work on viruses, because they do not have the same cell parts.” Little compared the two shapes again. Different tiny guests needed different kinds of help.
beats.prompt: Why doesn’t an antibiotic work on a virus?

beats.title: A clue to remember
beats.passage: “Your immune system is your body’s team of defenders,” said Big. “Some learn to recognize germs and remember them next time.” Little saved a shape in the notebook, then a command: “Rinse your hands well.” What other kind habits could Little keep?

math.title: Six small stories to solve
math.intro: Count bubbles, yogurt cups, and little drawings. Choose addition or subtraction for each story.

tasks.prompt: Little draws 28 soap bubbles, then draws 17 more. How many bubbles are on the page?
tasks.hint: Add the tens and ones. You may trade 10 ones for a ten.
tasks.worked: 28 + 17 = 45. Add 10 to reach 38, then add 7 to reach 45.
tasks.label: TASK 1

tasks.prompt: Little plans to scrub for 20 seconds. So far, 8 seconds have passed. How many seconds of scrubbing remain?
tasks.hint: Count up from 8 to 20, or subtract 8 from 20.
tasks.label: TASK 2

tasks.prompt: A breakfast shelf has 24 yogurt cups. Big adds 18 cups. How many yogurt cups are on the shelf now?
tasks.hint: Add 10 cups, then add 8 more cups.
tasks.worked: 24 + 18 = 42. First reach 34, then add 8 to reach 42.
tasks.label: TASK 3

tasks.prompt: Little draws 52 helpful bacteria in a notebook and colors 16 of them. How many drawings still need color?
tasks.worked: 52 − 16 = 36. Subtract 10 to reach 42, then subtract 6 to reach 36.
tasks.label: TASK 4

tasks.prompt: One book page shows 35 helpful bacteria. Another page shows 27. How many bacteria are shown on the two pages?
tasks.worked: 35 + 27 = 62. Add 20 to reach 55, then add 7 to reach 62.
tasks.label: TASK 5

tasks.prompt: Little has 63 bubble stickers and uses 25 on a handwashing poster. How many stickers are left?
tasks.worked: 63 − 25 = 38. Subtract 20 to reach 43, then subtract 5 to reach 38.
tasks.label: TASK 6

math.extension: Choose one story. Explain why you added or subtracted.
math.parentNote: Age 8 / Grade 2 math. Six one-step story problems within 100, with three additions and three subtractions. Offer counters, tens-and-ones drawings, or spoken reasoning.
math.actionLabel: Solve one story at a time
math.printNote: Show your thinking with a drawing, numbers, or words.

writing.title: Give a kind habit its words
writing.intro: Write one clear command sentence about washing hands. You can say it first.
writing.draw: Draw one handwashing step. Add one label.

frames.hint: tell how to use soap and scrub
tell how to rinse or dry

writing.check: Read your sentence. Does it tell what to do, with a command such as Wet, Scrub, Rinse, or Dry?
writing.parentNote: Accept a spoken command, dictation, invented spelling, or writing. One clear sentence is enough. Example: “First wet your hands, then scrub with soap for 20 seconds.”

answers.label: Reading · 1
answers.text: A bacterium is a whole living cell. A virus is smaller and is not a cell; it carries instructions in a coat and needs a living cell’s machinery to make copies.

answers.label: Reading · 2
answers.text: Soap can pull apart oily layers of many germs and helps loosen them from skin. Scrubbing helps lift them, and running water carries them away.

answers.label: Reading · 3
answers.text: Some defenders remember a germ’s features. Remembering can help them recognize the same germ faster next time.

answers.label: Writing
answers.text: Accept one sensible command, spoken, dictated, or written. Example: “First wet your hands, then scrub with soap for 20 seconds.”

parentGuidance: Leo is age 8: Grade 3 reading and Grade 2 math. Grown-ups and doctors decide about medicine. Many bacteria are helpful. Soap disrupts oily membranes of susceptible germs; it does not break apart every bacterium or every virus. Scrubbing and rinsing remove germs too. The diorama compares a bacterium and a virus with an oily outer layer; its removal amounts are qualitative, not measured. Antibiotics differ in which bacteria they affect and do not act on viruses. Immune memory helps recognition but is not a promise of complete protection.

authoring.learningRule: Leo is age 8, Grade 3 for reading; math is Grade 2. New Curiosity packs declare mathTemplate and require exactly six tasks for that template. Every number (operands, terms, intermediates, answers) is an integer from 0 to 100. Each task asks one clear question tied to the day's story and includes an equation matching the validated numbers, a hint, numeric answer, and short worked explanation containing the answer (mixed-review retains its shipped calculation rule). Replace scaffold notebook objects with the day's story objects. Explain precise vocabulary in context; welcome speech and dictation. Template story-problems: Six one-step word problems, each asking one question. Exactly two structured operands; both addition and subtraction appear. No two-step problems. Prose may spell out quantities or include context such as the day number.
